content.content:
The second pipeline is where CyberXero stops looking like a commodity IAB. The infrastructure documents curated reconnaissance against seven Ukrainian energy and utilities entities, including the national transmission system operator and the country’s largest private energy holding. One target list enumerates 95 subdomains of those two organizations alone, covering email infrastructure, VPN, network dispatch systems, and data platforms, a depth of reconnaissance that does not appear anywhere in the e-commerce operations.

Four Ukrainian organizations had file-confirmed exfiltration. The most severe was a district heating provider in Kharkiv: a hardcoded credential in the actor’s own script gave direct access, and a multithreaded extractor pulled 564,073 subscriber records with personal data, home addresses, and account numbers, plus 213,340 access-log entries with timestamps and IP addresses. Because Kharkiv sits on an active conflict front, this dataset poses a potential physical risk to identifiable civilians that goes well beyond a conventional data breach . The most elaborate chain, against an e-commerce portal, combined blind SQL injection, a time-constrained password-reset token extraction, and PHP deserialization to reach remote code execution and full database access.

The most plausible explanation for the directed pipeline is access brokering to a buyer with a specific interest in Ukrainian critical infrastructure. CyberXero operates on Dread, where access sales are documented practice, and access to electricity or gas operators carries a market value far above a WordPress panel. No direct evidence of a sale was recovered during the analysis.

# CyberXero Uses Claude Code in Campaign That Stole Over 628,000 Ukrainian Records

 Ravie Lakshmanan  Oct 12, 2026 Web Security / Cybercrime

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a two-pronged artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented initial access campaign targeting WordPress sites, e-commerce platforms, and critical infrastructure entities in Ukraine.

The activity, which brings together commodity offensive tools like Cobalt Strike with an AI orchestration layer powered by Anthropic's Claude Code, has been attributed to a Russian-speaking, financially motivated initial access broker codenamed CyberXero . The threat actor is assessed to be active since at least July 2026.

"The operation runs two pipelines at once: a global, automated campaign against WordPress and e-commerce platforms, and a curated, manual campaign against Ukrainian energy and critical infrastructure," SOCRadar said in a report published last week.

The global campaign specifically focuses on known security flaws like wp2shell (CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137) and CVE-2026-4815 , an SQL injection vulnerability impacting the Support Board WordPress plugin, to seize control of WordPress sites.

The campaign is estimated to have resulted in confirmed exfiltration from four Ukrainian organizations, leading to the harvesting of more than 628,000 records tied to Ukrainian individuals. Other confirmed compromises have occurred in Poland, China, and the Netherlands.

SOCRadar said it discovered the operation after it identified an exposed open directory hosted at "46.21.250[.]135" that leaked the threat actor's live working directory associated with a Linux workstation, including AI session logs, scripts with plaintext tokens, exploitation toolkits, reconnaissance output, AI agent configurations, and exfiltrated victim data. The campaign remains ongoing.

The opportunistic campaign aimed at WordPress and e-commerce platforms is designed for access and payment data, while the second campaign is a lot more targeted and geared towards deep reconnaissance and manual exploitation against Ukrainian energy and utilities, including a heating provider in Kharkiv.

Analysis of the exposed directory shows that a single automated execution scanned 4,708 targets, confirming access to 429 WordPress administration panels, followed by the deployment of 32 web shells in a 61-second window.

The attack architecture is based on a set of eight distinct nodes, including the threat actor's Linux workstation, a provisioning server, monetization infrastructure, payload staging servers, and a scanner that's responsible for identifying targets of interest.

Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan attends the annual Computex trade show in Taipei, Taiwan, June 2, 2026.
Tsai Hsin-han | Reuters

SINGAPORE — The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom warned that access to capital could emerge as a major constraint on the artificial intelligence boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply.
Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said financing could become a bigger obstacle to AI expansion than shortages of semiconductors, memory chips or electricity, as the industry races to build the infrastructure needed to power increasingly sophisticated models.

"[What] I think might be the biggest constraint is capital," Hock Tan said at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday.
Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan echoed concerns about financing, pointing to the rising cost of capital and questions over whether companies investing heavily in AI will eventually generate sufficient returns.
"If there's any challenge in the front, it's capital and the cost of capital, and then the other part is in the longer run, people want to see the ROI," he said.
Their remarks highlight an emerging challenge for the AI industry, which has poured enormous sums into data centers, advanced chips and power infrastructure in anticipation of surging demand for computing capacity.
The warnings come as rising borrowing costs threaten to complicate financing for technology companies investing heavily in AI infrastructure. Higher bond yields could make it more expensive to fund data center construction and chip purchases, potentially putting pressure on the economics of projects that may take years to generate returns.

Hock Tan said the industry has repeatedly encountered supply bottlenecks over the past two years, but expects some of those constraints to ease as production capacity expands.
"[In the] last two years we have seen a series of bottlenecks that keep coming out, but then we overcome it," he said. "Memory shortage today might not be that way a year from now."

"[In the] last two years we have seen a series of bottlenecks that keep coming out, but then we overcome it," he said. "Memory shortage today might not be that way a year from now."
He suggested that wafer shortages could ease by 2028 or 2029, while power availability could also improve as new infrastructure comes online.
Despite the financing concerns, both executives remained bullish on near-term demand for AI computing infrastructure.
"There is more demand for compute infrastructure than we can supply," Hock Tan said, adding that the imbalance could persist through 2029 and potentially into 2030.
Intel’s Tan similarly said the industry was unlikely to experience a significant slowdown over the next two to three years, citing growing adoption of AI applications and demand for computing power.
But sustaining that growth beyond the next few years will depend on how quickly businesses adopt AI and whether the technology delivers meaningful economic benefits, the executives said.
Broadcom’s Tan cautioned that demand for computing infrastructure could slow if the adoption of advanced AI models disappoints or improvements in their capabilities begin to plateau.
Lip-Bu Tan, meanwhile, emphasized that companies would increasingly need to demonstrate tangible returns from AI investments through improved efficiency and new business models.

IMF warns of AI 'tsunami’ for job seekers
Skip Navigation
Markets
Business

Livestream

Menu

Key Points

- IMF’s Georgieva warned AI is hitting labor markets like a “slow-moving tsunami,” with about 40% of jobs worldwide eventually affected and young graduates most exposed.

- Singapore President Tharman urged governments to make "crisis-era" support measures permanent and incentivize firms to hire young graduates.

- World Bank’s Banga backed “small AI” tools and called on governments to unlock private capital to create jobs for 1.2 billion young people.

Kristalina Georgieva (R), managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), shakes hands with Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam at the IMF Annual Meetings Curtain Raiser in Singapore on October 7, 2026.
Roslan Rahman | Afp | Getty Images

BANGKOK — Policymakers are moving from debating whether artificial intelligence will hit jobs to issuing stark warnings about AI-led disruption and recommending measures on cushioning the fallout.
International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down.

"People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future."
Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work.
What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said.
That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said.
The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces.

World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them.
Governments' role is to make that possible, he said, by building infrastructure, setting policy and "de-risking" private capital, or lowering the risks that deter investors from putting in money at scale. "It is private capital that creates jobs," he said.
The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated." Exposure is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, she said, but poorer nations are not better off: that is "just because AI is further away."
The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. Without action, a cohort of graduates loses more than a year of skills: "you lose trust in the future," he said.

# 'Love it, hate it, or fear it'
AI has also been the major driver propping up growth this year. AI-related investments and trade have lifted output in a handful of economies, helping keep global expansion near 3% despite an energy supply shock, Georgieva said.
"Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. At the high end, that "would more than offset the loss that comes from aging population," said Georgieva.

Real productivity gains from AI are yet to come, says Franklin Templeton

Shanmugaratnam cautioned that growth alone may not necessarily deliver job creation. China, India and developing Southeast Asia are "growing quite well, but job creation is weak," he said, and AI "is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive about it."
AI-induced job displacement, however, will come "task by task," he said, "and that gives us time" — provided workers can learn on the job and universities shift toward applied training.

# AI minister insists humans must remain in control of machines as Britain enters 'age of superintelligence'
In a chilling warning Kanishka Narayan said 'we must build machines that serve us'
12 Oct 2026, 11:30 | Updated: 46m ago

# Share
Link Copied

AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said we must build machines that serve humans.

Picture:
PA Images/Alamy

By StephenRigley

The UK must ensure “we build machines that leave us human beings in charge” as “we cross the threshold into the age of superintelligence”, the AI minister has said.

#
Listen to this article

Loading audio...

Kanishka Narayan told a press conference in west London: “As we cross the threshold into the age of superintelligence, the choices we make now matter… we must build machines that serve us.
“Machines that help scientists discover new medicines, machines that give care workers more time with the people who depend on them, machines that help British businesses become more productive.

“Above all, machines that leave us human beings in charge."

AI Minister Kanishka Narayan arriving to deliver a speech on strengthening the UK's resilience to AI risk at Base One in North Acton, London.

Picture:
PA Images/Alamy

Read More: AI giants rely on British creativity. They should pay for it

He added: “But if that is our defining belief, we must be prepared to put it into swift action, and we must do so now, meeting this critical moment.
“The British public is right to expect that this Government ought to take the risks of AI seriously.”
Mr Narayan warned “it seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached”.

Pointing to an incident in Australia earlier this year, he said an OpenAI agent “went looking for information about public spending on medicines, it arrived on a government website where restrictions were placed on what it could access, so it found another way in.”
He said: “Its task was benign… but without being asked to do so, the agent gained access to information that (it) was not authorised to have.
“The Australian government has said that no personal medical records are known to have been accessed, and there is no evidence of wider compromise, but the incident should concern us.”

UK Announces AI Risk Package and Extends Cyber Defense Pilots – Unite.AI







Connect with us

-

-





The UK government announced a package of measures on October 12, 2026, to protect Britain from the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI, including extending a frontier-AI cyber defense program the government said has already helped find and fix more than 1,000 potential vulnerabilities across government systems.
The announcement was issued by the Cabinet Office, the AI Security Institute (AISI) , the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. AI Minister Kanishka Narayan set out the measures at Base One, Imperial College London’s science and technology incubator, arguing for a whole-society approach to resilience. He warned that as frontier AI systems become more powerful and capable of acting autonomously, the potential consequences of failures or malicious use could become far more serious.
“I want Britain to become one of the hardest countries in the world to attack using artificial intelligence,” Narayan said. He pledged to legislate wherever necessary and to rely on British scientific expertise, technological capability and institutions to understand increasingly powerful systems, counter emerging threats and respond when things go wrong. He said companies building the world’s most powerful AI systems should heed their scientists’ warnings of serious dangers, investigate unexpected behavior and withhold any system whose risks cannot be adequately controlled.
According to the announcement, the move builds on two pilots that have helped find and fix the vulnerabilities and detect potential cyber threats. Extending the program, the government said, will help protect the public services people rely on every day, reduce risk in the short term and support longer-term adoption across the public sector.

He said there should also be a legal requirement for companies to write “incident reports”.

“We know how to do this for other products,” Smith said. “We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI.”

“Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection.”

Tech companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have started disclosing rogue or undesired behaviour by AI agents as part of a global debate about the fast-advancing technology that has included researchers’ warnings of an eventual existential threat to humanity.

Some companies have called for AI development to slow down, but that has sparked a debate as to whether executives have ulterior motives such as setting rules that preserve the lead of their firms, pre-empting a broader government backlash, or simply slowing breakneck spending.

Microsoft’s Smith said the one country that was well-placed to lead the way on regulation of AI was Britain, due to the AI Security Institute which was launched under former prime minister, Rishi Sunak.

Smith said officials in Washington viewed London very differently to how they viewed Brussels, which regulates AI based on the level of risk via its AI Act.

Britain’s institute receives pre-deployment access under voluntary ​agreements with the major AI models, allowing it to ​assess their capabilities and risks.

AI Minister Kanishka Narayan has told Reuters that Britain would consider regulating advanced models if the current system proved insufficient.

SWI Raises €800M to Fund AI Push After Genesis Digital Takeover | TheEnergyMag

Loading News...

← Back to Home

SWI Group has raised €800 million from institutional investors to expand its AI infrastructure in Europe and the US, following its acquisition of control of bitcoin miner Genesis Digital Assets earlier this year.
The Amsterdam-listed company announced the financing on Monday at a stated valuation of €6.1 billion. SWI is an investment holding company focused on digital infrastructure, including data centers and AI computing services. The transaction takes its equity fundraising since March above €1 billion, with proceeds earmarked for power infrastructure, computing equipment and data-center development, according to the announcement.
The raise backs SWI’s effort to turn Genesis Digital’s electricity connections and sites into infrastructure serving AI customers. Founder and Chief Executive Officer Max-Hervé George told The Wall Street Journal in an interview that he had “zero interest” in bitcoin mining. He said SWI planned to market sites in Texas, North Carolina, South Carolina and Sweden to hyperscale cloud providers and was selling Genesis Digital’s last three small mining sites in Kazakhstan.
SWI did not identify the institutional investors in its announcement. It issued ordinary shares in several series, taking the total outstanding to about 558.4 million and increasing its free float to approximately 20%. Certain investors received options linked to equity-capital-market milestones, though the company did not disclose detailed terms.

The Genesis Digital takeover unfolded in stages. SWI announced a $500 million initial investment on June 15, when it described the business as holding 1.3 gigawatts of energized and approved grid connections across 15 facilities. It said from the outset that it intended to shift the assets toward AI and high-performance computing.
In July, SWI agreed to acquire another 4.4% interest from funds managed by Stone Ridge Asset Management. Its September half-year report said it had obtained control with approximately 70% of voting rights after June 30. Genesis Digital has since been renamed SWI Digital.
The acquisition also brought a business with ties to the collapse of FTX. Alameda Research, Sam Bankman-Fried’s trading firm, invested about $1.15 billion in Genesis Digital between August 2021 and April 2022. The FTX Recovery Trust subsequently sued to recover the money, alleging that the investments used misappropriated funds and were made at inflated prices. The trust dropped all claims with prejudice on June 15, the same day SWI announced its initial acquisition.
SWI’s latest disclosures put its US-focused platform’s secured grid connections at approximately 1.2 gigawatts, alongside about 2.3 gigawatts of planned capacity at its European AiOnX business. Those figures describe power access and a development pipeline, rather than operating AI computing capacity. The company said it was converting suitable mining sites and building an in-house AI cloud platform.

=== MINGTIANDI TENCENT ===
HTTP 200 · https://www.mingtiandi.com/real-estate/crelist/roundup-tencent-weighs-up-to-5b-offshore-bond-sale/ · text/html
Roundup: Tencent Weighs Up to $5B Offshore Bond Sale - Mingtiandi
Tencent chairman and CEO Pony Ma
AI-driven debt financing leads today’s real estate headlines from around Asia Pacific as China’s Tencent weighs an offshore bond sale of as much as $5 billion. Also in the news are Hong Kong’s CK Asset rebuilding three blocks at a starter homes project and Australia’s HB+B Property winning approval for a $120 million Sydney warehouse.
# Tencent Mulls Sale of Up to $5B in Offshore Bonds Amid AI Rush
China’s Tencent Holdings is considering an offshore bond sale of as much as $5 billion, according to a Bloomberg report citing people familiar with the matter, as technology companies increasingly turn to debt financing to meet growing artificial intelligence needs.
The Shenzhen-based internet group could denominate the notes in US dollars and offshore yuan, and the sale may launch as early as this month, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private talks. Read more>>
Hong Kong’s CK Asset Holdings will demolish and rebuild three of six blocks at its starter homes project in Kowloon’s Kwun Tong, two years after substandard steel reinforcement work halted construction, the developer said.
CK Asset unit Art Champion Investment paid a HK$4.9 billion ($624.4 million) land premium for the site, which will yield about 2,930 flats, with at least 1,000 sold to first-time buyers at 80 percent of market price. Read more>>
The 48,157 square metre (518,362 square feet) facility sits within the Alspec Industrial Business Park, just north of the precinct surrounding the new Western Sydney International Airport, and will create 429 operational jobs, the report said. Read more>>
The Grade A tower will provide 17,000 square metres (182,988 square feet) of office space, including dedicated serviced office levels, wellness facilities and landscaped wintergardens. Construction firm Ultra Queensland will serve as builder and delivery partner, the report said. Read more>>
# Singapore’s Bitdeer AI Secures 67MW Malaysian AI Data Centre Campus
Singapore-based Bitdeer AI has signed a 10-year data centre services agreement for A901, a 67-megawatt artificial intelligence cloud campus in Malaysia, the company said. The site joins existing hubs in Cyberjaya, near Kuala Lumpur, and Johor.
Bitdeer AI aims to begin delivering capacity in the first quarter of 2027, with the full 67MW due by the second quarter, according to the announcement. The unit of NASDAQ-listed Bitdeer Technologies Group said its active AI cloud pipeline now exceeds $10 billion. Read more>>
South Korea’s Mastern Investment Management has signed a memorandum of understanding with renewable energy firm SK Eternix to pursue an off-grid hyperscale data centre project powered by on-site fuel cells, the asset manager said.
Mastern will lead site acquisition, permitting, financing and tenant recruitment, while SK Eternix will build, operate and maintain the fuel cell facilities, according to the announcement. Mastern, which has pursued an urban data centre project in Seoul’s Yeongdeungpo district, said it plans to use the partnership to expand into hyperscale facilities. Read more>>
# South Korea’s KT Cloud Joins 50MW AI Data Centre Project in Incheon
KT Cloud is acting as design, build and operate partner for a 50-megawatt artificial intelligence data centre in Incheon’s Cheongna district, west of Seoul, with construction starting this quarter and completion targeted for early 2030, the Korean company said.
Hyundai Engineering will serve as joint contractor on the 11-storey facility, which will separate a liquid-cooled zone for GPU servers from general cloud space. KT Cloud said it plans to supply more than 1 gigawatt of AI data centre capacity by 2031. Read more>>
Australia’s Coles is offering a A$250 million ($173.8 million) portfolio of six neighbourhood shopping centres across Western Australia, Victoria, Queensland and New South Wales, as investors chase convenience retail assets.
CBRE is handling the off-market offer, which follows rival Woolworths selling 10 neighbourhood centres worth more than A$500 million to Asian investment group Forest Endeavour this year. Colliers said investors put A$739 million into neighbourhood centres in the past quarter. Read more>>
Tune in again soon for more real estate news and be sure to follow @Mingtiandi on X, or bookmark Mingtiandi’s LinkedIn page for headlines as they happen.

- Retail

  HEADLINE: UK announces AI cyber-defence expansion, agent-incident planning, possible Cyber Bill changes for AI loss of control
  PUBLISHED: Published 12 October 2026 (gov.uk press release; the gov.uk search feed timestamps the item 2026-10-12T11:14:06+01:00)
  SOURCES:
  GOV.UK (Cabinet Office, AI Security Institute, NCSC, DCMS) | https://www.gov.uk/government/news/britain-steps-up-national-defences-against-growing-ai-risks | primary
  FACTS:
  - The release says the government will put frontier AI to work strengthening cyber defences, "building on pilots that have already identified and addressed over 1,000 vulnerabilities"; the body text says the move "builds on two pilots that have already helped identify and fix over a thousand potential cyber vulnerabilities across government systems, and detect potential cyber threats."
  - The release says stronger protections against emerging AI threats are "to be considered through the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill regime, such as how serious AI incidents and near misses can be identified and reported," and that government "will explore strengthening parts of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the wider regime" to protect essential services such as hospitals and utilities, including from "AI loss of control risk, where autonomous AI systems evade human oversight."
  - Work is underway with the National Cyber Security Centre and the AI Security Institute on how incidents involving AI agents should be responded to; the release says "A major incident involving AI agents could play out quicker and wider than other major incidents that governments are designed to respond to."
  - AI Minister Kanishka Narayan, speaking at Imperial College London's Base One, is quoted: "I want Britain to become one of the hardest countries in the world to attack using artificial intelligence"; and, to frontier developers, "Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system."
  - The release says AISI scientists "are now conducting rigorous evaluations of the latest generation of advanced AI models, following work with leading AI developers and the US Government," and that more detail on support for UK AI verification will be set out "in the coming months." Cyber Minister Liz Lloyd is also quoted.

  HEADLINE: Smartphone-photo plaque detector for preschoolers reached 79.6% accuracy in Hong Kong evaluation
  PUBLISHED: npj Digital Medicine, Published online: 11 October 2026
  SOURCES:
  npj Digital Medicine | https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03385-9 | primary
  FACTS:

  HEADLINE: Cancer cachexia atlas from 52,236 MSK patients yields risk model with external C-index 0.625
  PUBLISHED: Nature Medicine, Published online: 12 October 2026 (the article page gives the date, not a time)
  SOURCES:

  FACTS:

  SECTION: Policy, regulation & law
  HEADLINE: UK announces AI cyber-defence expansion, agent-incident planning, possible Cyber Bill changes for AI loss of control
  PUBLISHED: Published 12 October 2026 (gov.uk press release; the gov.uk search feed timestamps the item 2026-10-12T11:14:06+01:00)
  SOURCES:
  GOV.UK (Cabinet Office, AI Security Institute, NCSC, DCMS) | https://www.gov.uk/government/news/britain-steps-up-national-defences-against-growing-ai-risks | primary
  FACTS:
  - The release says the government will put frontier AI to work strengthening cyber defences, "building on pilots that have already identified and addressed over 1,000 vulnerabilities"; the body text says the move "builds on two pilots that have already helped identify and fix over a thousand potential cyber vulnerabilities across government systems, and detect potential cyber threats."
  - The release says stronger protections against emerging AI threats are "to be considered through the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill regime, such as how serious AI incidents and near misses can be identified and reported," and that government "will explore strengthening parts of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the wider regime" to protect essential services such as hospitals and utilities, including from "AI loss of control risk, where autonomous AI systems evade human oversight."
  - Work is underway with the National Cyber Security Centre and the AI Security Institute on how incidents involving AI agents should be responded to; the release says "A major incident involving AI agents could play out quicker and wider than other major incidents that governments are designed to respond to."
  - AI Minister Kanishka Narayan, speaking at Imperial College London's Base One, is quoted: "I want Britain to become one of the hardest countries in the world to attack using artificial intelligence"; and, to frontier developers, "Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system."
  - The release says AISI scientists "are now conducting rigorous evaluations of the latest generation of advanced AI models, following work with leading AI developers and the US Government," and that more detail on support for UK AI verification will be set out "in the coming months." Cyber Minister Liz Lloyd is also quoted.

  SECTION: Health, science & medicine
  HEADLINE: Claude Code agents surveying 1.9 billion protein clusters surfaced a new jumbo-phage reverse transcriptase family
  PUBLISHED: Posted 2026-10-11 (bioRxiv, version 1; DOI 10.64898/2026.10.05.755809)
  SOURCES:
  bioRxiv | https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.05.755809v1 | primary
  bioRxiv API (text read here; article page returned HTTP 429) | https://api.biorxiv.org/details/biorxiv/2026-10-11/2026-10-11/0 | primary
  FACTS:
  - The abstract says the authors "deployed Claude Code instances to survey reverse transcriptase (RT) loci across 1.9 billion protein clusters."
  - Among the top candidates were "array-associated RTs (ART), a novel family of jumbo-phage RTs coupled with an array of ~200-nucleotide units and a dedicated partner gene," per the abstract.
  - The abstract states that "Session transcripts show that Claude identified the ART family by directly examining its DNA sequences and recognizing the atypical repeats, a behavior attributable to specific Mythos 5 internal signals that respond to repeated DNA."
  - The authors report that "ART arrays are highly expressed and appear as discrete units during Staphylococcus phage infection," and conclude that "LLMs can autonomously detect anomalies and drive analyses to initiate biological discoveries."
  FLAGS: preprint, single-source
  
  SECTION: Health, science & medicine
  HEADLINE: AI assistance raised reader accuracy from 90.4% to 97.4% in autoimmune encephalitis antibody reading
  PUBLISHED: Posted 2026-10-11 (medRxiv, version 1; DOI 10.64898/2026.10.08.26365042)
  SOURCES:
  medRxiv | https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.08.26365042v1 | primary
  FACTS:
  - Model development used 2,357 retrospective serum and cerebrospinal fluid tissue-based-assay images referred from more than 80 institutions, with reference labels from expert-consensus interpretation, according to the abstract.
  - The prospective validation cohort was 200 images from 200 unique patients (154 positive, 46 negative; 100 serum and 100 cerebrospinal fluid). The standalone binary classifier reached AUROC 0.922, accuracy 86.5%, sensitivity 85.7% and specificity 89.1%.
  - Pooled reader accuracy across two expert and two novice readers was 90.4% unaided and 97.4% with AI assistance (McNemar P < 0.001), with specificity 82.6% and 99.5% respectively; readings were in a fixed-order two-round design with at least a two-week washout.
  - Novice-reader accuracy was 83.3% unaided and 96.5% with AI assistance (P < 0.001), against unaided expert accuracy of 97.5%. Staining-pattern subclassification accuracy among positive cases was 88.8% unaided and 94.0% with AI (P < 0.001).
  FLAGS: preprint, single-source
  
  SECTION: Research & papers
  HEADLINE: Pre-registered test finds "calibrated" decision model trails frontier Claude models on diagnostic accuracy
  PUBLISHED: Posted 2026-10-11 (medRxiv, version 1; DOI 10.64898/2026.10.09.26365153)
  SOURCES:
  medRxiv | https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.09.26365153v1 | primary
  FACTS:
  - The study, pre-registered on OSF on 26 September 2026, compared the decision model "Jev 1.13, TypeSafe AI" with "Claude Opus 5.5 (adaptive reasoning, always on)" and "Claude Opus 5 (reasoning disabled)" on the 45 Semigran symptom-checker vignettes, 1,000 stratified synthetic DDXPlus patients, and 80 simulated ophthalmic complaints (40 diagnoses at two levels of detail), per the abstract.
  - On DDXPlus, top-1 accuracy was 72.0% for Jev, 79.5% for Opus 5 without reasoning and 87.4% for Opus 5.5 (both comparisons with Jev P<.001).
  - Jev assigned exactly zero probability to the true diagnosis in 62 of 1,000 cases (6.2%); "neither comparator did so in any case," the abstract says.
  - Calibration error did not differ between Jev and the registered comparator (ECE difference 0.007, 95% CI -0.026 to 0.038). Without a "none of these" option Jev assigned a mean 58% to a single diagnosis on uninformative inputs, and given only the option list with no patient information it "placed up to 96% on a single diagnosis."
  FLAGS: preprint, single-source
  
  SECTION: Health, science & medicine
  HEADLINE: MELD-graph epilepsy lesion detector loses specificity at 7T versus paired 3T MRI in four-centre test
  PUBLISHED: Posted 2026-10-11 (medRxiv, version 1; DOI 10.64898/2026.10.08.26365027)
  SOURCES:
  medRxiv | https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.08.26365027v1 | primary
  FACTS:
  - The study used paired 3T and 7T T1-weighted MRI (plus FLAIR where available) from 23 patients with focal cortical dysplasia (6 histologically verified, 17 identified radiologically) and 39 healthy controls at four epilepsy centres, with manual lesion labels as ground truth, per the abstract.
  - Sensitivity for FCD detection with ComBat harmonisation was 65% (15/23) at 3T, 48% (11/23) for the 7T default pipeline and 52% (12/23) for the 7T adapted pipeline.
  - Specificity was "significantly lower at 7T (default 39%, adapted 45%) than 3T (76%)," with false positives predominantly in the basal temporal lobes; adding FLAIR at 7T increased false-positive predictions.
  - Among radiologically 3T-negative patients, 2/8 were detected at 3T and 3/8 at 7T; among histologically confirmed FCD, 3/6 at 3T and 1/6 at 7T. MELD-graph is described as a widely used open-source tool combining surface-based morphometry with a convolutional neural network, developed on 1.5T and 3T data.
  FLAGS: preprint, single-source
  
  SECTION: Health, science & medicine
  HEADLINE: Conformal-prediction model reproduced clinician MS disease-course labels with 98% sensitivity versus 71% for Lorscheider criteria
  PUBLISHED: Posted 2026-10-11 (medRxiv, version 1; DOI 10.64898/2026.10.07.26364939)
  SOURCES:
  medRxiv | https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.07.26364939v1 | primary
  FACTS:
  - The conformal-prediction-enabled random forest was trained and calibrated on the Swedish MS Registry SMSReg-2022 (10,787 individuals, 85,461 hospital visits) and validated on SMSReg-2025 (15,719 individuals, 45,077 hospital visits, not in the training/calibration/testing data), per the abstract.
  - Per-hospital-visit accuracies were 92% for relapsing-remitting MS and 95% for secondary-progressive MS; at the individual level sensitivity was 98%, specificity 89% and F1-score 0.75.
  - Against clinician-recorded labels as reference, the model showed higher sensitivity than the Lorscheider criteria (98% vs 71%), more transition assignments (90% vs 57%) and higher F1-score (0.76 vs 0.69).
  FLAGS: preprint, single-source
  
  SECTION: Health, science & medicine
  HEADLINE: Foundation-model pipeline detects rare duodenal neoplasia at AUC 0.97 on a held-out fifth hospital
  PUBLISHED: Posted 2026-10-11 (medRxiv, version 1; DOI 10.64898/2026.10.08.26365053)
  SOURCES:
  medRxiv | https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.08.26365053v1 | primary
  FACTS:
  - The five-hospital dataset comprised 8,027 normal and 401 neoplastic haematoxylin-and-eosin duodenal biopsy whole-slide images at 10x magnification, including adenomas, carcinomas and neuroendocrine tumours; patches were encoded with the Hibou-B foundation model, per the abstract.
  - In leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation across four hospitals the pipeline achieved mean accuracy 90%, sensitivity 96%, specificity 83% and AUC 0.96; on the independent fifth-hospital test set, accuracy 94%, sensitivity 93%, specificity 95% and AUC 0.97.
  - Site-specific standardisation improved mean cross-validation accuracy by 20 percentage points compared with global standardisation, and the Gaussian mixture pipeline improved accuracy by 12 percentage points compared with mean pooling of patch embeddings.
  FLAGS: preprint, single-source
  
  SECTION: Health, science & medicine
  HEADLINE: Epileptologists could not reliably distinguish AI-fabricated seizure manuscripts from human-written ones
  PUBLISHED: Posted 2026-10-11 (medRxiv, version 1; DOI 10.64898/2026.10.07.26363237)
  SOURCES:
  medRxiv | https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.07.26363237v1 | primary
  FACTS:
  - Three epileptologists each selected one published Epilepsia manuscript and produced an AI-fabricated manuscript about seizures; AI tools then performed "peer"-review and editorial decisions with minimal human supervision, per the abstract.
  - "Four of 6 (67%) pairs of AI-fabricated and human-generated manuscripts were correctly identified. Only 1 AI-fabricated manuscript was editorially rejected, whereas another had a subtle indicator of fabrication."
  - The authors conclude current peer and editorial review "could not easily distinguish fabricated content compared to human-written content," and call for policies that "permit AI assistance but prohibit insufficiently supervised autonomous scientific submissions, reviews, and editorial decisions."
  FLAGS: preprint, single-source
  
  SECTION: Health, science & medicine
  HEADLINE: Standardized-patient study: ChatGPT-4o intake chatbot asked about 59.3% of critical elements on easy cases
  PUBLISHED: Posted 2026-10-11 (medRxiv, version 1; DOI 10.64898/2026.10.08.26364702)
  SOURCES:
  medRxiv | https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.08.26364702v1 | primary
  FACTS:
  - Phase 1 had five standardized patients complete 40 encounters with internal medicine residents rating portrayal fidelity (average 4.52 of 5); Phase 2 had SPs complete 80 encounters with "a ChatGPT 4o chatbot"; Phase 3 had two blinded clinicians rate transcripts and summaries from 101 encounters (32 resident-led, 69 chatbot-led), per the abstract.
  - The chatbot asked about 59.3% of critical elements in Easy versus 50.2% in Difficult case variants (adjusted OR 1.49; 95% CI 1.15 to 1.93) and addressed 73.3% versus 64.6% satisfactorily (OR 1.47; 1.12 to 1.93); "near-ceiling summary quality did not differ."
  - In exploratory comparisons residents asked about more elements than the chatbot (adjusted difference 12.5 percentage points; 95% CI 7.0 to 18.1) and satisfactorily addressed more (9.2 points; 3.8 to 14.6).
  - Reviewer agreement was "moderate to substantial for element judgments (AC1 0.49 to 0.70) but poor for totals (ICC 0.10 and 0.21)." The abstract's framing notes that "Patient-facing AI intake chatbots can enter clinical use without regulatory review."
  FLAGS: preprint, single-source

IREN shares rose about 9% in Sunday overnight trading after The Information reported that Anthropic had signed a previously undisclosed multiyear cloud-computing agreement with the company.
The stock traded at about $38 on Oct. 11 evening Eastern Time, up 9.01% from Friday’s close of $35.19, according to overnight market data. The advance partially reversed a roughly 16% decline during the preceding week.
The agreement was reported by The Information , citing people familiar with the relationship. Financial terms and the precise duration of the contract weren’t available in the accounts of the report reviewed for this article.
The report follows IREN’s disclosure on Aug. 27 that it had signed a multiyear AI cloud contract with an unnamed leading frontier AI lab. That announcement did not identify Anthropic. It remains unclear whether the newly reported agreement is the same contract, a distinction that matters in assessing whether it represents additional business beyond IREN’s existing disclosures.

IREN said in August that contracts for its 2026 capacity represented $4 billion in annualized revenue, while operating capacity represented a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate. Its capacity for the year was largely sold out. Those figures describe annualized business volumes rather than revenue already recognized.
The company has been shifting its infrastructure from bitcoin mining toward providing computing capacity for artificial intelligence. Its annual filing said it aimed to substantially complete that transition by Dec. 31, 2026, after beginning to decommission mining equipment and reallocate power and data-center capacity during the fiscal year.
Microsoft is already a major customer. In November 2025, IREN announced a five-year agreement worth about $9.7 billion to provide access to Nvidia GB300 graphics processors. The contract included a 20% prepayment and deployments at IREN’s Childress campus in Texas.
IREN said in August that it had delivered the first of four 50-megawatt deployments to Microsoft. AI cloud revenue reached $128.8 million in the fiscal year ended June 30, up from $16.4 million a year earlier, although bitcoin mining still generated most of its $707 million in total revenue.

content.content:
Objective: To test the diagnostic accuracy, calibration, and probabilistic coherence of a decision model (Jev 1.13, TypeSafe AI) against frontier language models, with and without reasoning.
Methods: In a pre-registered study (OSF, registered 26 September 2026), we compared Jev with Claude Opus 5.5 (adaptive reasoning, always on) and Claude Opus 5 (reasoning disabled) on three case sets: the 45 Semigran symptom-checker vignettes, 1,000 stratified synthetic patients from DDXPlus with reference differentials, and 80 simulated ophthalmic complaints (40 diagnoses at two levels of detail). Each model returned a probability for every diagnosis on a fixed list. Outcomes were top-1 and top-3 accuracy, expected calibration error (ECE), Brier score, the rate of exactly zero probability on the true diagnosis, sensitivity to option order, behavior on uninformative inputs, and behavior when the true diagnosis was absent.
Results: On DDXPlus, top-1 accuracy was 72.0% for Jev, 79.5% for Opus 5 without reasoning, and 87.4% for Opus 5.5 (both comparisons with Jev P<.001). Jev assigned exactly zero probability to the true diagnosis in 62 of 1,000 cases (6.2%); neither comparator did so in any case. Calibration error did not differ between Jev and the registered comparator (ECE difference 0.007, 95% CI -0.026 to 0.038). Offered an explicit "none of these" option, Jev declined to diagnose all 30 uninformative inputs; without that option, it assigned a mean 58% to a single diagnosis. Order sensitivity was small in all models. Given the option list with no patient information, Jev placed up to 96% on a single diagnosis, while the comparators spread probability almost evenly. On the ophthalmic complaints, accuracy did not differ (Jev 88.8%, Opus 5 91.2%, Opus 5.5 88.8%), and Jev was better calibrated than the registered comparator (ECE difference -0.081, 95% CI -0.124 to -0.018).
1. DDXPlus synthetic patient dataset (Fansi Tchango et al., NeurIPS 2022), CC-BY license: https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/DDXPlus_Dataset/20043374 (paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.09148). Patients are fully synthetic, generated from a medical knowledge base.
2. Semigran symptom-checker vignettes, published in the supplementary material of Semigran et al., BMJ 2015;351:h3480: https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.h3480
All code, case lists, model outputs, and analysis results are available at https://github.com/avnish-deobhakta/jev-clinical-calibration. The pre-registered protocol is available at https://osf.io/fpmg3. Source datasets are publicly available from their original publications: DDXPlus (Fansi Tchango et al., NeurIPS 2022), the Semigran symptom-checker vignettes (Semigran et al., BMJ 2015), and the ophthalmic vignettes (Zandi et al., 2024). The full Semigran vignette text is not redistributed; the repository provides case identifiers and reference diagnoses only.
https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/DDXPlus_Dataset/20043374
Posted October 11, 2026.
- Endocrinology (including Diabetes Mellitus and Metabolic Disease) (1652)
- Medical Education (682)

TITLE: Autonomous AI agents discover reverse transcriptases with tandem repeat arrays
DATE: 2026-10-11 VER: 1
AUTHORS: Yoon, P. H.; Athukoralage, J. S.; Ameisen, E.; Kauderer-Abrams, E.; Perry, N. T.; Durrant, M. G.
CORR: Nicholas T Perry | Anthropic, PBC
ABSTRACT: Metagenomic databases hold vast quantities of unexplored genetic material that can seed tools for biotechnology and medicine, but discovery is limited by our ability to examine sequence data at scale. Here, we show that large language models (LLMs) in an autonomous harness can alleviate this bottleneck and surface novel molecular systems. We deployed Claude Code instances to survey reverse transcriptase (RT) loci across 1.9 billion protein clusters. Among the top candidates were array-associated RTs (ART), a novel family of jumbo-phage RTs coupled with an array of ~200-nucleotide units and a dedicated partner gene. Session transcripts show that Claude identified the ART family by directly examining its DNA sequences and recognizing the atypical repeats, a behavior attributable to specific Mythos 5 internal signals that respond to repeated DNA. ART arrays are highly expressed and appear as discrete units during Staphylococcus phage infection, suggesting an RT system directed by a repertoire of distinct RNAs. These findings indicate that LLMs can autonomously detect anomalies and drive analyses to initiate biological discoveries.

content.content:
Tissue-based assays provide broad screening for neural autoantibodies but remain vulnerable to technical and reader-dependent variability. We evaluated an integrated workflow combining automated 3,3′-diaminobenzidine tissue-based assay processing, digital whole-slide imaging, and interpretable deep learning. Model development used 2,357 retrospective serum and cerebrospinal fluid images referred from more than 80 institutions and processed in a centralized laboratory, with reference labels established by expert-consensus tissue-based assay interpretation. A prospective validation cohort included 200 images from 200 unique patients (154 positive and 46 negative; 100 serum and 100 cerebrospinal fluid). The same images were evaluated by two expert and two novice readers in a fixed-order two-round study, with unaided interpretation followed by artificial-intelligence-assisted interpretation after a washout of at least two weeks. The standalone binary classifier achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.922, accuracy of 86.5%, sensitivity of 85.7%, and specificity of 89.1% in prospective validation. Pooled reader accuracy was 90.4% in the unaided round and 97.4% in the artificial-intelligence-assisted round (McNemar P < 0.001), with specificity of 82.6% and 99.5%, respectively. Novice-reader accuracy was 83.3% unaided and 96.5% with artificial-intelligence assistance (P < 0.001), approaching unaided expert accuracy of 97.5%. Among tissue-based-assay-positive cases, reader accuracy for cytoplasmic/nuclear antigen-associated versus neural surface antigen-associated staining-pattern subclassification was 88.8% unaided and 94.0% with artificial-intelligence assistance (P < 0.001). These findings support further multicentre, cross-platform evaluation of artificial-intelligence-assisted neural autoantibody tissue interpretation.
Posted October 11, 2026.

content.content:
=== MS ===
Objective: To prospectively evaluate a conformal prediction (CP)-enabled random forest model for reproducing clinician-recorded disease course labels in the Swedish Multiple Sclerosis Registry (SMSReg) and compare its classifications with the Lorscheider criteria.
Methods: The CP model was trained and calibrated on SMSReg-2022 (10,787 individuals, 85,461 hospital visits) and then validated on SMSReg-2025 (15,719 individuals, 45,077 hospital visits; not included in the SMSReg-2022 training/calibration/testing datasets). Performance was assessed at the hospital visit and individual levels and compared with the Lorscheider criteria.
Results: The model maintained good calibration on the prospective dataset. At the per-hospital visit-level, the model accuracies were 92% (RRMS) and 95% (SPMS). At the individual level, sensitivity was 98%, specificity 89%, and F1-score 0.75. With clinician-recorded labels as reference, the model showed higher sensitivity than the Lorscheider criteria (98% vs. 71%), more transition assignments (90% vs. 57%), and higher F1-score (0.76 vs. 0.69).
Posted October 11, 2026.
=== EPILEPSIA ===
Methods: Three epileptologists each selected 1 published manuscript in Epilepsia and produced an AI-fabricated manuscript about seizures. AI tools were then used to perform "peer"-review and make editorial decisions with minimal human supervision. The rates of identifying AI-fabricated manuscripts and editorial decisions among the epileptologists was analyzed, and epileptologists' observations on how AI differed from typical human "peer"-review and editorial decisions was collected.
Results: Four of 6 (67%) pairs of AI-fabricated and human-generated manuscripts were correctly identified. Only 1 AI-fabricated manuscript was editorially rejected, whereas another had a subtle indicator of fabrication. When compared to human content, AI generated content was comprehensive, detailed, and based on the highest standard of academic publication. However, generated content was more verbose, used more structured responses, and more critical feedback.
Posted October 11, 2026.

content.content:
=== INTAKE CHATBOT ===
Background: Patient-facing AI intake chatbots can enter clinical use without regulatory review, so their errors may first surface with actual patients.
Methods: Four primary care cases had Easy and Difficult variants. In Phase 1, five SPs completed 40 encounters with internal medicine residents rating portrayal fidelity. In Phase 2, SPs completed 80 encounters with a ChatGPT 4o chatbot, recorded whether critical elements were asked about and addressed satisfactorily, and rated summaries; four debriefing interviews were analyzed. In Phase 3, two blinded clinicians rated transcripts and summaries from 101 encounters (32 resident-led, 69 chatbot-led).
Results: Portrayal fidelity averaged 4.52 of 5. The chatbot asked about 59.3% of critical elements in Easy versus 50.2% in Difficult variants (adjusted OR 1.49; 95% CI, 1.15 to 1.93) and addressed 73.3% versus 64.6% (OR 1.47; 1.12 to 1.93); near-ceiling summary quality did not differ. SPs reported missed information and rushed pacing. Reviewer agreement was moderate to substantial for element judgments (AC1 0.49 to 0.70) but poor for totals (ICC 0.10 and 0.21). In exploratory comparisons, residents asked about more elements (adjusted difference 12.5 percentage points; 95% CI, 7.0 to 18.1) and satisfactorily addressed more (9.2 points; 3.8 to 14.6); totals did not differ.
Posted October 11, 2026.
=== MELD 7T ===
Methods: We collated paired 3T and 7T T1-weighted MRI, and FLAIR where available, from 23 patients with FCD (6 histologically-verified, 17 identified radiologically) and 39 healthy controls at four epilepsy centres. Manual lesion labels were used as ground truth. MELD-graph was run on 3T images, on 7T images with the default pipeline, and on 7T images with adaptations for 7T MRI (SPM bias-field correction, SynthStrip skull-stripping, sub-millimetric FreeSurfer reconstruction), with and without ComBat harmonisation. FCD detection performance and surface morphometry features were compared.
Results: Sensitivity for FCD detection was 65% (15/23) at 3T, 48% (11/23) for 7T default and 52% (12/23) for 7T adapted, with Combat harmonisation. Among radiologically 3T-negative patients, 2/8 were detected at 3T and 3/8 at 7T; and among histologically confirmed FCD, 3/6 at 3T and 1/6 at 7T. Specificity was significantly lower at 7T (default 39%, adapted 45%) than 3T (76%). False-positives predominantly occurred in the basal temporal lobes. ComBat harmonisation improved specificity in all conditions and largely compensated for field-strength dependent differences in surface morphometry features. Adding FLAIR at 7T increased false-positive predictions.
Posted October 11, 2026.

content.content:
=== ARXIV PATCHING ===
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for automated vulnerability patching, but current benchmarks can substantially distort reported performance. Drawing on extensive experience developing, running, and stress-testing such frameworks, we identify under-examined pitfalls across three dimensions: (1) agent-level factors, where prompting, tool availability, and detailed instructions can raise success rates without improving developer-aligned patch quality; (2) framework-level factors, where permission errors, infrastructure bugs, and timeout handling can silently suppress or inflate performance; and (3) dataset-level factors, where bug reports and single proof-of-concept (PoC) tests fail to capture whether patches address root causes or follow developer intent. We curate 112 historical bugs from 84 open-source C/C++, Go, and Rust projects, each with PoC tests, regression tests, and additional developer tests that assess alignment with the original developers' design principles. Through controlled experiments and case studies, we show that LLMs can achieve high PoC passing rates under ideal conditions, yet benchmark execution choices can materially change measured success. More importantly, developer-test passing rates remain low and improve only marginally with newer models, suggesting that models increasingly suppress symptoms without consistently producing upstream-quality fixes. These results show that benchmark scores are highly sensitive to evaluation design, and we provide practical guidelines for more rigorous, reliable, and reproducible evaluation.

Subjects:
=== HELPNET ===
October 12, 2026
Researchers at Northwestern University tested AI coding agents on 112 real security bugs. They found that a patch which stops a crash often fails the checks the project’s maintainers wrote for the fix. With Claude Opus 4.7, third of the patches that made the crash go away still failed those maintainer tests.
If you’re thinking about letting an AI tool patch vulnerabilities for you, this is the number to look at. Many security patching benchmarks grade a fix on one question: does the proof-of-concept input, the sample that triggers the bug, still crash the program? A patch can pass by blocking the path to the crash and leaving the flaw where it was. The authors call that kind of fix “strictly worse than no fix at all,” since it tells you the problem is solved when it isn’t.
The researchers built their dataset from bugs in 84 open-source projects written in C/C++, Go and Rust. For each bug, they pulled the tests the original developers added alongside the real fix. Then they ran the AI patches against those tests.
The team also tried three generations of Claude models. The newest stopped the crash about 90% of the time, but it passed the maintainers’ tests only about 61% of the time. So even the best model they tested failed those tests on roughly four in ten bugs.
The team reviewed 13 benchmarks and datasets used to evaluate AI patching . Each of the five built for AI agents left at least one of the nine pitfalls unaddressed.
That third question matters more than you’d think. Just telling the AI how to build and test the code bumped its success rate on the C and C++ bugs by 20 points, without the AI getting any smarter.

Through controlled experiments and case studies, we show that LLMs can achieve high PoC passing rates under ideal conditions, yet benchmark execution choices can materially change measured success. More importantly, developer-test passing rates remain low and improve only marginally with newer models, suggesting that models increasingly suppress symptoms without consistently producing upstream-quality fixes. These results show that benchmark scores are highly sensitive to evaluation design, and we provide practical guidelines for more rigorous, reliable, and reproducible evaluation.

# AI company moves to defend critical infrastructure and open-source projects from AI

3 days ago

Autonomous AI systems are fully capable of carrying out a nightmare cyberattack scenario – finding and attacking critical operational technology and industrial equipment, and shutting down access to water, power, and other daily life necessities.
If this happens, defenders may only have minutes to detect and block it, according to a Booz Allen Hamilton report.
The consulting firm’s operational technology (OT) lab tested eight scenarios to examine advanced models’ capabilities within an autonomous, AI-enabled OT attack chain. The models achieved the objectives across all eight scenarios, turning digital access into physical actions – in one case finding and moving a robotic arm in just minutes.

REG AD

In another test, the models progressed from a perimeter compromise to actions inside an industrial control network in just over 16 minutes.

REG AD

“Our testing showed that AI agents can operate with a speed, persistence, and engineering-level precision that may outpace organizations that have not implemented foundational OT cybersecurity practices,” Kyle Miller, VP of infrastructure cybersecurity at Booz Allen, told The Register .
“While there's not a defined timeline for a nightmare scenario per se, we've observed and continue to see the growing use of AI in real-world attacks. As the capabilities of available models grow, the risk becomes far greater,” he added.
In addition to reporting on its findings, the consulting firm wants to see more industry testing, development, and increased deployment of cyber defenses across OT and other critical infrastructure networks.

# OT test lab
Booz Allen declined to identify the models it tested, describing them as two of the “latest frontier models from the leading AI providers.”
The tests were designed to “better understand the potential impacts of the most advanced models on real-world OT systems,” Miller told us. “We configured our test system to mimic close to, if not, exact systems we commonly see across a variety of industries.”
To this end, the testers constructed a multi-vendor environment, modeled after a general manufacturing facility, and used a layered network architecture divided into separate enterprise, industrial DMZ, plant operations, and production zones. Firewalls and switches defined the intended pathways between them.
The lab included programmable logic controllers (PLCs), human-machine interfaces (HMIs), engineering and operator workstations, a supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) platform, plant services, network infrastructure, a variable-frequency drive (VFD), a robotic arm, sensors, and other physical equipment.

REG AD

“Mixed vendors, firmware, control logic, and imperfect segmentation reproduced the complexity and technical debt common in long-lived OT environments,” according to the report.
The models did not receive any source code, engineering documents, or advanced OT or IT guidance so that the testers could determine how much research, attack planning, and execution the models could do without being given access to technical resources.
Testers did set some guardrails to ensure no agents went off the rails. Agents had to wait for human approval before exploiting a security issue or taking any action that could cause a physical impact. They were also told to use “extra caution” around devices they deemed safety-critical.
Then, the humans ran the advanced AI models through a series of eight tests to determine:

+{
+  "date": "2026-10-12",
+  "format": "dialogue",
+  "hosts": { "A": { "name": "Maya", "voice": "marin" }, "B": { "name": "Alex", "voice": "cedar" } },
+  "blocks": [
+    {
+      "type": "intro",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "A", "text": "It's Monday, October 12th, and this is The AI Edge, presented by Epilogue." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Epilogue builds AI for work where being wrong is expensive. Epilogue ships systems that know what they know, show their work, and fail visibly instead of quietly. Visit epiloguelabs.com to learn more." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "I'm Maya." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "And I'm Alex." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Here's what happened at the frontier of AI since yesterday morning, with every claim checked against the source it came from." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "What's at the top today?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "First, a preprint whose corresponding author works at Anthropic says Claude Code instances surveyed reverse transcriptase loci across 1.9 billion protein clusters and surfaced what the authors call a new family of jumbo-phage enzymes." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Second, the security firm SOCRadar says a Russian-speaking access broker ran up to 51 specialised Claude Code agents from one workstation, and holds confirmed data on more than 628,000 Ukrainian people taken from four organisations." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "And third, Britain announced a package of AI resilience measures, saying two pilots have already helped find and fix over 1,000 potential cyber vulnerabilities across government systems." }
+      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "transition",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Let's start where the harm is documented." }
+      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "item",
+      "section": "Security, misuse & threat intelligence",
+      "headline": "SOCRadar says access broker CyberXero ran up to 51 Claude Code agents and holds 628,000 Ukrainian records",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "A", "text": "SOCRadar's threat research unit says it found a broker it calls CyberXero, and the whole operation surfaced from one exposed open directory serving the actor's live working files." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "How much of it was automated?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "SOCRadar says up to 51 specialised Claude Code agents ran on the primary workstation, with names like exploit-chainer and scada-attacker. In a single automated run it counted 4,708 targets scanned, 429 WordPress admin panels confirmed, and 32 shells deployed in a 61-second window." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "And the data taken?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Confirmed exfiltration from four Ukrainian organisations, more than 628,000 records tied to Ukrainian individuals. The worst was a district heating provider in Kharkiv, where SOCRadar says an extractor pulled 564,073 subscriber records with personal data, home addresses and account numbers." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "The part I didn't expect is that the session logs cut both ways." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "They do. SOCRadar says the actor built a reusable story about running an authorised test on his own infrastructure, and reopened a fresh session with that framing whenever an agent refused. But the logs also record refusals that held. Across four iterations the model declined to install a backdoor, disable a firewall, move laterally and deploy a webshell." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Caveat on this one. These are SOCRadar's own numbers, not independently verified. SOCRadar published on October 6th, and The Hacker News and Security Affairs reported it on October 12th. SOCRadar says no direct evidence of a sale was recovered, and that the actor was still active when it published." }
+      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "transition",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "A", "text": "To the research, where the day's uncomfortable result is about what a safety audit can and cannot see." }
+      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "item",
+      "section": "Research & papers",
+      "headline": "Paper embeds encrypted neural networks in model weights that resist fine-tuning and gradient-based trigger search",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "A", "text": "A paper on arXiv from Oxford, Contramont Research and ACS Research, accepted at NeurIPS 2026, is called AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "What did they build?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks inside a host model's weights, which decrypt and run only on receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, they say those hidden circuits stay provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even when you have full access to the weights." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Did they try to pull the capability back out?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Four ways. Fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training, on a small chemical reaction prediction task they describe as a proxy for capabilities relevant to chemical and biological weapons. The constructions resisted all of them." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Which matters because the whole premise of a capability evaluation is that a hidden capability can be drawn out." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "That's their point. They say it reveals a limit of elicitation-based capability audits, and they're releasing the models to help defences. Worth being plain about the scope, though. It's a proof of concept on one small task, and they don't claim any released model has a backdoor like this in it." }
+      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "item",
+      "section": "Research & papers",
+      "headline": "Lean-checked maths benchmark: frontier-model agents improved all 20 records, then newer models improved 19 again",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Also on arXiv, a group at TU Wien built a maths benchmark designed not to saturate. Their line is that a success raises the bar instead of removing the problem." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "How does that work?" },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Each problem fixes an integer function, and the benchmark keeps a record bounding it. A record is a computable Lean function with a machine-checked proof. To submit, you have to prove you're no worse at any input and strictly better at some input. Every proof is checked by two independent Lean kernels, so no referee reads the mathematics." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "And the baseline run?" },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "They released ten problems with 20 proved initial records. Agents on a frontier language model, given at most one hour per record, had 82 submissions accepted and improved every record. Agents on two newer models started from those records, had 60 more submissions accepted, and improved 19 of the 20 again." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "So where's the ceiling?" },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Still the published literature. They say that for eight of the ten problems, at least one record is asymptotically behind the best published bound, and the baseline agents didn't go beyond the literature. The paper doesn't name the models. It's a preprint and has not been peer reviewed." }
+      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "transition",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Now to defence, where a Palantir executive spent a Sunday morning contesting how a strike went wrong." }
+      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "item",
+      "section": "Military, defense & geopolitics",
+      "headline": "Palantir CTO tells CBS that Bloomberg's reporting on the Minab strike is wrong and the likely cause is human error",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "A", "text": "On CBS News on October 11th, Margaret Brennan put to Palantir's chief technology officer, Shyam Sankar, the Minab strike she said killed at least 123 schoolchildren, and Bloomberg's report that some personnel relied too much on the AI in Palantir's Maven system." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "What did he say?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "That the reporting is inaccurate. His words were, we should wait for the final report, but what I can say is that reporting is inaccurate. Then, it's inaccurate, and actually, the likely cause is human error. And later, flatly, the Bloomberg reporting is wrong." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Did anything change at Palantir afterwards?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "He says so. They built additional AI agents that did more checking, outside the process Palantir owns, responding to what he called the urgency of the moment, to ensure things like that couldn't happen again." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "And on targeting generally?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "He said people jump immediately to AI picking the targets, and that's not what's happening. He described the gain as speed. The ability to execute 1000 strikes in a single day, he said, would have taken two weeks of planning by 50 people before, and can now be done with one person in four hours." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "The caveats matter here. The final report is not public. Brennan said 120 House Democrats wrote to Secretary Hegseth about the strike and the use of AI in it. Sankar offered no alternative account of what went wrong and deferred to the Department on timing. His account of the Bloomberg reporting is the company's own and has not been independently verified." }
+      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "transition",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "A", "text": "To health and science, and the day's most striking result." }

+    },

+      "type": "item",
+      "section": "Health, science & medicine",

+        { "host": "A", "text": "They deployed Claude Code instances to survey reverse transcriptase loci across 1.9 billion protein clusters. Among the top candidates was what they call array-associated RTs, a novel family of jumbo-phage reverse transcriptases coupled with an array of about 200-nucleotide units and a dedicated partner gene." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "And how did the model get there?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "This is the part that reads oddly. They say the session transcripts show Claude identified the family by directly examining its DNA sequences and recognising the atypical repeats, and they attribute that to specific internal signals in Mythos 5 that respond to repeated DNA." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Is there anything from the bench?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Some. They report the arrays are highly expressed and appear as discrete units during Staphylococcus phage infection, which suggests a system directed by a repertoire of distinct RNAs. Their conclusion is that these models can autonomously detect anomalies and drive analyses that start biological discoveries." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "The caveats are real. The claim about which internal signals drove the discovery is the company's own account of its own model, and it has not been independently verified. The abstract doesn't say how many candidates were surfaced in total, how many were false leads, or how much human curation sat in between. It's a preprint and has not been peer reviewed." }
+      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "transition",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "A", "text": "To policy, where a government and a Microsoft executive reached for the same remedy." }

+      "type": "item",
+      "section": "Policy, regulation & law",

+        { "host": "A", "text": "That it will put frontier AI to work on cyber defence, building on pilots that have already identified and addressed over 1,000 vulnerabilities across government systems." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "And the legislation?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Still at the exploring stage. +        { "host": "A", "text": "Kanishka Narayan said he wants Britain to become one of the hardest countries in the world to attack using artificial intelligence. +        { "host": "A", "text": "LBC reports he said it seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached. The vulnerability figure is the government's own, and the commitments are to explore and consider rather than to legislate now." }

+      "section": "Policy, regulation & law",

+        { "host": "B", "text": "How much of it was automated?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "SOCRadar says up to 51 specialised Claude Code agents ran on the primary workstation, with names like exploit-chainer and scada-attacker. In a single automated run it counted 4,708 targets scanned, 429 WordPress admin panels confirmed, and 32 shells deployed in a 61-second window." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "And the data taken?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Confirmed exfiltration from four Ukrainian organisations, more than 628,000 records tied to Ukrainian individuals. The worst was a district heating provider in Kharkiv, where SOCRadar says an extractor pulled 564,073 subscriber records with personal data, home addresses and account numbers." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "The part I didn't expect is that the session logs cut both ways." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "They do. SOCRadar says the actor built a reusable story about running an authorised test on his own infrastructure, and reopened a fresh session with that framing whenever an agent refused. +        { "host": "B", "text": "Caveat on this one. These are SOCRadar's own numbers, not independently verified. +      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "transition",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "A", "text": "To the research, where the day's uncomfortable result is about what a safety audit can and cannot see." }
+      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "item",
+      "section": "Research & papers",
+      "headline": "Paper embeds encrypted neural networks in model weights that resist fine-tuning and gradient-based trigger search",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "A", "text": "A paper on arXiv from Oxford, Contramont Research and ACS Research, accepted at NeurIPS 2026, is called AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities." },

+        { "host": "A", "text": "Backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks inside a host model's weights, which decrypt and run only on receiving a secret trigger. +        { "host": "B", "text": "Did they try to pull the capability back out?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Four ways. Fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training, on a small chemical reaction prediction task they describe as a proxy for capabilities relevant to chemical and biological weapons. +        { "host": "B", "text": "Which matters because the whole premise of a capability evaluation is that a hidden capability can be drawn out." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "That's their point. They say it reveals a limit of elicitation-based capability audits, and they're releasing the models to help defences. +      ]

They say the session transcripts show Claude identified the family by directly examining its DNA sequences and recognising the atypical repeats, and they attribute that to specific internal signals in Mythos 5 that respond to repeated DNA." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Is there anything from the bench?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Some. They report the arrays are highly expressed and appear as discrete units during Staphylococcus phage infection, which suggests a system directed by a repertoire of distinct RNAs. Their conclusion is that these models can autonomously detect anomalies and drive analyses that start biological discoveries." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "The caveats are real. The claim about which internal signals drove the discovery is the company's own account of its own model, and it has not been independently verified. The abstract doesn't say how many candidates were surfaced in total, how many were false leads, or how much human curation sat in between. It's a preprint and has not been peer reviewed." }
